name: Panic attack / anxiety

matching.reasoningTemplate: Palpitations, chest tightness and breathlessness in a young patient with normal workup may be a panic attack — but exclude organic causes.

redFlags: Do not anchor on anxiety until cardiac/pulmonary emergencies excluded

investigations.test: Diagnosis of exclusion — rule out ACS/PE first

harrison.pages: Harrison 22e p.103-107 (Chest Discomfort, Chap. 15); p.161, p.165 (Syncope/Dizziness); p.215 (Sleep Disorders); p.291 (Palpitations); p.376 (Hyperventilation syndrome / Respiratory Alkalosis)
clinicalPearls: Up to ~10% of patients presenting to emergency departments with acute chest discomfort have an underlying panic disorder or a related condition (p.104).

Psychiatric/emotional chest discomfort is variable in duration (fleeting to prolonged), often felt as chest tightness and breathlessness with a sense of panic or impending doom, and may be retrosternal; situational triggers and a prior history of panic attacks or depression support the diagnosis (p.103).
A psychiatric cause for palpitations is favoured when the sensation is reported as lasting longer (>15 min) and is accompanied by additional symptoms, in contrast to most arrhythmic causes (p.291).
Panic attacks can arise out of sleep and must be distinguished from parasomnias and other nocturnal events (p.215).

Apparent (psychogenic) loss of consciousness can occur in panic disorder and related conditions; suspect it in patients who faint frequently without prodrome, are rarely injured despite repeated falls, and have no concurrent hemodynamic change (no hypotension/bradycardia) during the event (p.161).
harrison.pathophysiology: Acute attacks are commonly accompanied by hyperventilation; the resulting hypocapnia (Paco2 often 15-30 mmHg) produces an acute respiratory alkalosis without hypoxemia, which underlies many of the somatic symptoms (paresthesia, circumoral numbness, chest-wall tightness, dizziness, air hunger, and rarely tetany) and can perpetuate the disorder. Catecholaminergic/hyperadrenergic activation contributes to palpitations and the hyperdynamic sensation (Harrison 22e p.376, p.291).
additionalDifferentials: Hyperventilation syndrome (respiratory alkalosis) — itself a diagnosis of exclusion (p.376)
Generalized anxiety disorder and somatization presenting with palpitations or pseudo-syncope (p.161, p.291)
Vasovagal syncope precipitated by fear/stress/anxiety (distinguished by accompanying hypotension +/- bradycardia, unlike psychogenic pseudo-syncope) (p.161)
Cataplexy / narcolepsy as a cause of episodic collapse (consciousness preserved) (p.161)
Persistent postural-perceptual dizziness (PPPD) and chronic subjective dizziness, in which anxiety disorders are common comorbidities (p.165)
nonInfectiousMimics: Acute coronary syndrome / myocardial ischemia (aching, heavy, squeezing retrosternal discomfort) (p.103)
Pulmonary embolism (chest discomfort, sinus tachycardia, ECG axis shift/S1Q3T3) (p.107)
Supraventricular or ventricular tachyarrhythmia and atrial fibrillation (palpitations) (p.291)
Hypoglycemia (tremor, palpitations, anxiety, diaphoresis, hunger, paresthesias from autonomic activation) (p.161)
Systemic mastocytosis; stimulant/drug effects (caffeine, cocaine, amphetamines, cannabis, ethanol); post-COVID syndrome — as causes of palpitations (p.291)
additionalInvestigations: Resting 12-lead ECG, with serial tracings, to exclude arrhythmia and ischemia in palpitations/chest discomfort (p.291); note hyperventilation in panic can itself produce nonspecific ST-segment and T-wave abnormalities (p.107)
Ambulatory rhythm monitoring (Holter, event/loop recorder, implantable loop recorder, or mobile cardiac outpatient telemetry) for infrequent recurrent palpitations (p.291)
Arterial blood-gas analysis when hyperventilation suspected: shows respiratory alkalosis with hypocapnia (Paco2 ~15-30 mmHg) but no hypoxemia (p.376)
redFlags: Normocapnia together with hypoxemia in a hyperventilating patient is a warning sign that may herald impending respiratory failure — do not assume benign anxiety (p.376)

High-risk syncope features that argue against a psychogenic cause: new chest discomfort, dyspnea, exertional or supine syncope, palpitations preceding syncope, structural/coronary heart disease (p.161)

Chest discomfort with features of an acute cardiopulmonary catastrophe (ACS, acute aortic syndrome, pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax, pericarditis with tamponade) must be excluded first (p.105)
pitfalls: Anchoring on anxiety/panic prematurely: because attacks mimic ACS, PE, arrhythmia, thyrotoxicosis, pheochromocytoma and hypoglycemia, organic emergencies must be excluded — panic disorder and the hyperventilation syndrome are diagnoses of exclusion (p.105, p.376).
Misreading hyperventilation-related nonspecific ST-segment/T-wave changes as evidence of ischemia (or vice versa) (p.107).
When ruling in a hyperventilation/psychiatric cause, still exclude pulmonary embolism, coronary artery disease and hyperthyroidism (p.376).

ECG, review drugs and substances, test for medical mimics
Recurrent attacks with 4+ symptoms and 1 month of worry or behaviour change?
Isolated panic attack; reassure and reassess if recurrent

Start CBT and or an SSRI or SNRI
